newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU agrees telecoms, satellite schemes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU agrees telecoms, satellite schemes.

text.p: European Union ministers on Friday agreed a key part of their plan to liberalise EU telecommunications markets, a regime for licensing companies once state monopolies are ended.
They also agreed to coordinate the regulation of satellite systems that will begin to offer mobile phone and data-transmission services by the end of the decade.
Both initiatives must be approved by the European Parliament before final adoption.
The telecoms licensing plan requires governments to use open and objective procedures and establishes a "one-stop shopping" system for companies wanting to operate in more than one EU state.
A final sticking point was over when to oblige operators to apply for individual licences and when to allow them to fall under a "general authorisation" scheme requiring no prior approval.

The European Commission wanted to restrict the use of individual licences to cases where governments needed to allocate radio frequencies or numbers, grant access to land or impose public service obligations.
But the ministers decided EU states should be allowed to require individual licences as well for all providers of voice telephone services or public telecommunications networks, EU officials said.

They also agreed that governments should be able to limit the number of operators in a given sector only if needed to ensure the efficient use of radio frequencies or, on a temporary basis, because of a shortage of telephone numbers.
That responded to a request from Spain, which said it needed more time to reorganise its numbering system as required under previous EU legislation.
The text says governments must in principle decide on applications for individual licences within six weeks, although that could be extended up to eight months in cases of competitive bidding.

On satellite personal communications services, the ministers agreed a watered-down plan that would give primary responsibility to the inter-governmental European Conference for Postal and Telecommunications Administrations (CEPT).

The European Commission had hoped to set up a single EU system for selecting and authorising the satellite systems that will begin by the end of the decade to offer mobile phone and data communications services.
However, EU member states in earlier discussions resisted the plan because it would have allowed the Commission to draw up criteria for licensing operators and to play a major role in selecting them.

EU officials said the ministers endorsed a new text that asks CEPT to take a series of actions by mid-1997, including harmonising the use of frequency bands and the procedures for authorising the new systems.
The legislation also asks the Commission and CEPT to set up a "one-, stop-shopping" system to make it easier for operators to get authorised in more than one EU state at the same time.
The ultimate decision on whether to allow a communications system to operate from national territory -- that is, to set up a satellite uplink -- rests with individual EU states.
The text asks EU states to coordinate their decisions, however, if the number of systems must be limited because of a shortage of frequencies.

It also says the EU can step in if the Commission or a member state consider that CEPT's work is not progressing satisfactorily. The decision would be taken by a licensing committee composed of the Commission and national representatives that will be set up under separate legislation on telecoms licences.

EU states would be required to implement the telecommunications licensing regime by December 31, 1997, just in time for the January 1, 1998 EU deadline for liberalising all telecoms sectors in most countries.
The satellite plan would take force 20 days after it is published in the EU's Official Journal.
